replying_to: Replying to Mimicking Randomized Controlled Trials to Learn End-to-End Patient Representations through Self-Supervised Covariate Balancing for Causal Treatment Effect Estimation
display_title: Official Review of Paper1700 by Reviewer FRNd

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed a new method for causal treatment effect estimation through self-supervised covariate balancing. The main contribution of the paper is to adopt the auto-balancing self-supervised loss function to learn the balancing score (like the propensity score).
content.main_review:
1. The whole Section 3.1. just presents existing results, which looks redundant. In particular, it is not clear why Theorem 5 needs to be included here. It is completely disconnected with the proposed method. 

2. The major selling point of the proposed method is to use the auto-balancing self-supervised loss function to learn the weight function g. It is not clear why this is better than the binary cross-entropy loss function considered in the literature. Some discussions of the intuition or theoretical justifications should be provided. 

3. The asymptotic distribution of the proposed estimators of ATE/ATT and their associated variance estimation methods are not considered in this paper. 

4. In experiments, the tuning parameter $\lambda_{BAL}$ was set as 1. Is this a recommended choice for all applications? Is a data-driven method necessary selecting the optimal $\lambda_{BAL}$ in practical applications?
content.summary_of_the_review: My main concern is the novelty of the work. Compared with existing approaches, the only difference of the proposed method is to use the auto-balancing self-supervised loss function to learn the weight function g (similar to the propensity score function). However, its intuition and theoretical justifications are not provided.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1700 by Reviewer FRNd

content.title: Response to Reviewer FRNd
content.comment:
We’d like to thank the reviewer for the valuable feedback. 

As evidenced by another reviewer raising similar issues, we have indeed not 
clearly articulated our main contributions and we have revisited our 
manuscript with an updated introduction e conclusion. Although our model
improves upon the previously SOTA Dragonnet,
our main finding is that what was previously considered a best practice when
estimating propensity scores, which was the adoption of the binary-cross-entropy (BCE) objective, framing the problem as a supervised one, has been misunderstood to 
some extent and it is not supported by the early findings of Rosenbaum and 
Rubin (1983). In their seminal work, Rosenbaum and Rubin propose a 
framework for estimating treatment effects using propensity scores observed
from the data while suggesting a model candidate (a logit model). 
Modeling the propensity scores in a supervised manner does not appear to be a main conclusion of their work. Their analysis aims at mimicking randomized control trials and a different optimization goal is more appropriate based on later work by Shalit et al. (2017b), who discovered an upper bound on the expected PEHE for representation learning models. Our main contribution is reevaluating the original premise of propensity score modeling to closer mimicking randomized control trials and the use of representation learning techniques for achieving optimal results. Theorem 5 in our manuscript developed in Shalil et al. (2017b), provided the theoretical justification for our analysis. 

In addition, in supplementary section A.2 (“THE EFFECT OF BACK-PROPAGATING THE GRADIENT WITH RESPECT TO THE AUTO-BALANCING OBJECTIVE”) is shown in detail how the back-propagation works with our self-supervised objective to achieve minimal dissimilarity between treated and untreated representations, while in section A.3 (“COMPARISON WITH THE BINARY CROSS-ENTROPY OBJECTIVE”) the comparison with BCE is performed, showing why if we adopt the former instead of the latter we have a lower upper bound of the expected error in learning ITE (Theorem 5), in case the treated and untreated covariate distributions are highly dissimilar, as unfortunately might happen for observational data. 

We have deeply revised our manuscript to better reflect our main contributions. We believe that representation learning is important when estimating heterogeneous treatment effects, and often changing the training objective can lead to important changes in the learned representations. For instance, [1] contains many examples of this kind. In our case, adopting the self-supervised auto-balancing regularization term instead of the binary cross-entropy term leads to superior performance, and the reason for this is that such objective allows to learn treated and untreated representations more similar, as RCTs are designed to do, than previously published SOTAs. This, thanks to Theorem 5, implies a lower upper bound for the expected error in learning ITEs.

Regarding the asymptotic distribution of the proposed estimators of ATE/ATT,
we have not performed such analyses, which we would like to address in 
subsequent publications. As mentioned in Shalit et al. “...work differs from all
the above by focusing on the generalization-error aspects of estimating 
individual treatment effect, as opposed to asymptotic consistency...” which 
has provided the theoretical justification for using an IPM-like term 
(implemented using our self-supervising auto-balancing loss term).

On the topic of choosing $\mathcal{\lambda}_{BAL}=1$, this is indeed a hyper-parameter that 
should be tuned according to the data. We agree on the centrality of the hyper-parameter tuning and, indeed, in the revised manuscript the section 5.1 (“Ablations”) is devoted to this purpose. 
In this section (Table 2) we evaluated different values of  

* $\mathcal{\lambda}_{BAL}$   (relative importance of the self-supervised auto-balancing term), 

* $\mathcal{\lambda}_{BCE}$    (relative importance of the binary cross-entropy term), 

* $\mathcal{\lambda}_{TAR}$  (relative importance of the Dragonnet targeted regularization term) ,  

* different activation functions (ReLU, ELU, Tanh)

* different batch sizes and optimizers. 

We proved empirically and highlighted that the best combination of hyperparameters are the ones reported in sect. 4.3. Specifically on $\lambda_{BAL}=1$, row 13 and 14 of Table 2 show that the same optimal performance can be achieved when $0<\lambda_{BAL}<1$ and $1<\lambda_{BAL}<2$, if the network is regularized only with our self-supervised auto-balancing term.  


Thanks again for your thoughtful reviews and helpful suggestions!

Reference:

1. [Bengio et. al., Representation Learning: A Review and New Perspectives, IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence, 2013](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/6472238)

We acknowledge that our main contribution has not been clearly articulated. Although our model improves upon the previously SOTA Dragonnet, our main finding is that what was previously considered a best practice when estimating propensity scores, which was the adoption of the binary-cross entropy (BCE) objective, framing the problem as a supervised one, has been misunderstood to some extent and it is not supported by the early findings of Rosenbaum and Rubin [3]. In their seminal work, Rosenbaum and Rubin propose a framework for estimating treatment effects using propensity scores observed from the data while suggesting a model candidate (a logit model). Modeling the propensity scores in a supervised manner does not appear to be a main conclusion of their work. Their analysis aims at mimicking randomized control trials and a different optimization goal is more appropriate based on later work by Shalit et al. [4], who discovered an upper bound on the expected PEHE for representation learning models. Our main contribution is reevaluating the original premise of propensity score modeling to closer mimicking randomized control trials and the use of representation learning techniques for achieving optimal results. Theorem 5 in our manuscript developed in Shalil et al. [4], provided the theoretical justification for our analysis. 

In addition, in supplementary section A.2 (“THE EFFECT OF BACK-PROPAGATING THE GRADIENT WITH RESPECT TO THE AUTO-BALANCING OBJECTIVE”) is shown in detail how the back-propagation works with our self-supervised objective to achieve minimal dissimilarity between treated and untreated representations, while in section A.3 (“COMPARISON WITH THE BINARY CROSS-ENTROPY OBJECTIVE”) the comparison with BCE is performed, showing why if we adopt the former instead of the latter we have a lower upper bound of the expected error in learning ITE (Theorem 5), in case the treated and untreated covariate distributions are highly dissimilar, as unfortunately might happen for observational data. These are advanced topics and we had to put them in the appendix because of the constraint of max. 9 pages for the main part of the manuscript. 

We have deeply revised our manuscript to better reflect our main contributions. We believe that representation learning is important when estimating heterogeneous treatment effects, and often changing the training objective can lead to important changes in the learned representations. For instance, [1] contains many examples of this kind and [2] is the case of Denoising Auto-Encoders able to learn, just changing the training objective, not just to reconstruct the initial image, but to reconstruct the clean input from a corrupted version of an image. In our case, adopting the self-supervised auto-balancing regularization term instead of the binary cross-entropy term leads to superior performance, and the reason for this is that such objective allows to learn treated and untreated representations more similar, as RCTs are designed to do, than previously published SOTAs. This, thanks to Theorem 5, implies a lower upper bound for the expected error in learning ITEs. 

We hope our revised version addresses your concerns. Thanks again for your thoughtful review!

replying_to: Replying to Mimicking Randomized Controlled Trials to Learn End-to-End Patient Representations through Self-Supervised Covariate Balancing for Causal Treatment Effect Estimation
display_title: Official Review of Paper1700 by Reviewer b7Dh

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposed a new representation learning-based approach to estimate the treatment effects from observational data. The approach is based on modifying the existing Dragonnet developed by Shi et al. The new approach is called BCAUSS.

There are two terms in the objective of BCAUSS: 1) the first term aims to minimize the regression loss using the factual outcomes, which is the same as those used in Dragonet; and 2) the second term aims to minimize the mean square between the g-weighted covariates within the treatment and control group. In Shi's work, the second term makes use of the binary cross entropy to minimize the distribution distance between the treatment and control group in the representation space. Therefore, the second term of BCAUSS is different from Dragonnet and the new idea of this work.

Experimental results on one synthetic dataset, one semi-synthetic dataset (IHDP) and one real-world dataset (Jobs) demonstrate the proposed BCAUSS can achieve lower error in estimating the ATE and ATT.

Further analysis showed BCAUSS learns representations leading to more similar distributions between the treatment and control group compared to Dragonnet. The performance gain of BCAUSS compared to Dragonnet becomes greater when the distributions between the treatment and control becomes more dissimilar.
content.main_review:
The key contribution of this work, i.e., replacing the binary cross entropy term in the Dragonnet with the auto-balancing term in Eq. (2), seems quite incremental. 

My major complaint of this work is the lack of hyper parameter tuning for those baseline models. To fairly compare different approaches, it is essential to tune the hyper-parameters of baselines (even only Dragonnet in this case). Otherwise, it's hard to determine if the performance improvement of the proposed approach is due to a more appropriate hyper-parameter tuning or the objective function itself.

In Table 1, besides the error in estimating ATE and ATT, did the author compute the error of estimating ITE as well? If so, would the proposed approach still outperform the competing approaches?
content.summary_of_the_review:
Novelty: Limited novelty due to incremental modifications of existing work.
Experiments: Major flaws due to the lack of hyper-parameter tuning for baselines
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1700 by Reviewer b7Dh

content.title: Response to Reviewer b7Dh
content.comment:
We’d like to thank the reviewer for the valuable feedback. 
We completely agree on the need to highlight hyperparameter tuning and, indeed, in the revised manuscript the section 5.1 (“Ablations”) is devoted to this purpose. In this section (Table 2) we evaluated different values of  

* $\mathcal{\lambda}_{BAL}$   (relative importance of the self-supervised auto-balancing term), 

* $\mathcal{\lambda}_{BCE}$    (relative importance of the binary cross-entropy term), 

* $\mathcal{\lambda}_{TAR}$  (relative importance of the Dragonnet targeted regularization term) ,  

* different activation functions (ReLU, ELU, Tanh)

* different batch sizes and optimizers. 

We proved empirically and highlighted that the best combination of hyperparameters are the ones reported in sect. 4.3. 

Regarding the hyper-parameter tuning for Dragonnet, Row 0 of Table 2 corresponds to Dragonnet and the related results are worse in train/test accuracies compared to BCAUSS. For example, on test-set Dragonnet comes with an $\epsilon_{ATE}$ of $0.18\pm.01$ vs. $0.15\pm.01$ of BCAUSS.    However, the best hold-out result for Dragonnet in our analysis is significantly better than the one reported in the original paper [1],  e.g.  on test-set $\epsilon_{ATE}$ in [1]  is $0.20\pm.01$, obtained with lower batch size. In the supplementary Section A.3 (“COMPARISON WITH THE BINARY CROSS-ENTROPY OBJECTIVE”) we discuss in detail why working with large batch-size and SGD is beneficial for the binary cross-entropy objective. 

Regarding computing the errors of estimating ITEs in Table 1, although it is technically feasible for our model to predict ITEs, existing literature using the IHDP/Jobs datasets only provides metrics for ATE/ATT. Specifically, for the Jobs dataset we cannot evaluate PEHE, since there is no ground truth for the ITE. In literature as evaluation metrics are used $\epsilon_{ATT}$ or $R_{POL}$. We selected  the former, as it is easier to understand and to communicate. For the IHDP dataset, there were both options, i.e. $\epsilon_{PEHE}$ and $\epsilon_{ATE}$. However, our comparator for this dataset is Dragonnet and in [1] the latter is adopted. In order to directly compare against previously developed models and to also demonstrate SOTA error rates for our model (the previous SOTA on IHDP dataset was Dragonnet), we evaluated our model on the same metrics of our comparators. 

Regarding novelty, we acknowledge that our main contribution from this work has not been clearly articulated. Although our model improves upon the previously SOTA Dragonnet, our main finding is that what was previously considered a best practice when estimating propensity scores, which was the adoption of binary cross-entropy as objective, framing the problem as a supervised one, has been misunderstood to some extent and is not supported by the early findings of Rosenbaum and Rubin (1983). In their seminal work, Rosenbaum and Rubin propose a framework for estimating treatment effects using propensity scores observed from the data while suggesting a model candidate (a logit model). Modeling the propensity scores in a supervised manner does not appear to be a main conclusion of their work. Their analysis aims at mimicking randomized control trials and a different optimization goal is more appropriate based on later work by Shalit et al. (2017b), who discovered an upper bound on the expected error in learning ITEs for representation learning based models (Theorem 5). Our main contribution is reevaluating the original premise of propensity score modeling to closer mimicking randomized control trials and the use of representation learning techniques for achieving optimal results. Theorem 5 in our manuscript developed in Shalil et al. (2017b), provided the theoretical justification for our analysis. We have deeply revised our manuscript to better reflect our main contributions. We believe that representation learning is important when estimating heterogeneous treatment effects and that often changing the training objective can lead to significant changes in the learned representations. In our case, adopting the self-supervised auto-balancing regularization term instead of the binary cross-entropy term leads to superior performance, and the reason for this is that such objective allows to learn treated and untreated representations more similar (as RCTs are designed to do) than previously published SOTAs which, thanks to Theorem 5, implies a lower upper bound for the expected error in learning ITEs. 

We hope our revised version addresses your concerns. Thanks again for your thoughtful review!

 
Reference:

1. [Claudia Shi, David M. Blei, and Victor Veitch. Adapting neural networks for the estimation of treatment effects. In Hanna M. Wallach, Hugo Larochelle, Alina Beygelzimer, Florence d’Alche´ Buc, Emily B. Fox, and Roman Garnett (eds.), NeurIPS, pp. 2503–2513, 2019.](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2019/file/8fb5f8be2aa9d6c64a04e3ab9f63feee-Paper.pdf)

replying_to: Replying to Mimicking Randomized Controlled Trials to Learn End-to-End Patient Representations through Self-Supervised Covariate Balancing for Causal Treatment Effect Estimation
display_title: Official Review of Paper1700 by Reviewer uhL3

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper considers the problem of estimating causal effects (atomic interventions) under the canonical conditionally ignorable model. The authors use neural network-based outcome modeling, following several papers in the "causal learning community". The authors employ a novel loss function that aims to re-cast input covariates into a representation that achieves balance between the treatment and control groups. While this is a novel way to employ balancing and an intuitive use of representation learning, it is not clear what this method adds relative to simpler balancing + outcome model methods (like AIPW) that achieve balance directly/explicitly, have theoretical guarantees, and are generally less data hungry than neural network models.

Beyond this primary concern, aspects of the paper are somewhat poorly written. For instance, the language that attempts to justify combining balancing with outcome modeling is unclear on why this might be a good idea. The paper needs to be cleaned up substantially.
content.main_review:
Point by point comments numbered according to approximate order of appearance in the paper:
1) The authors' approach entails fitting separate models for treated and control groups. I am curious what their reason is for doing so? Generally there is some covariate information shared between the two groups and it is more statistically efficient to fit one model (i.e. regress Y on T and X and then plug in values of T when actually estimating) rather than two.
2) "Real World Data" -- I think it's more appropriate to use the expression "observational" data. RCT data is real and implying it is not is just going to confuse readers.
3) Throughout the citation formatting is done poorly. In many places a text citation is used where a parenthetical makes sense from context and it makes the flow of the paper very stilted. I'd advise alternating between \citep and \citet where appropriate.
4) "Footnote 1: BCAUSS roughly stands for 'Balancing Covariates Automatically using Self-Supervision'"? It either does or it doesn't. It's your method. There's no need for this footnote and the authors maybe shouldn't try so hard to come up with a buzzword name for their method if they have to say it "roughly" stands for some backronym.
5) Bottom of section 2: "In our work we don't make any assumptions on the generative process of the underlying covariate and outcome distributions". This is not true. The authors, in the next section, assume conditional ignorability and a variety of other (standard) conditions. This is not "assuming nothing". Perhaps the authors meant to say they don't make any _parametric_ assumptions?
6) "Bayesian" conditioning. I think the authors just mean condtioning?
7) "It is easy to see that x is the finest balancing score" --> what is meant by fine (or coarse) here? How can x be a balancing score if it's is conditionally independent of t given b(x)? The implication is if t and x are unconditionally independent then no re-balancing is needed?
8) Definition 2: if phi is injective and has an inverse, why not just say phi is bijective? Are the authors verifying that their learned representation is invertible?
9) Why use ReLU for some activations and sigmoid for others?
10) "incentivated" is not a word
11) The thrust behind using representation learning was not very clear until around the middle of section 3.2. The authors should make clearer what the goal of using rep learning is in this context. Beyond this point, it is not clear why this method should perform any better than fitting an AIPW estimator. In both cases (this method and AIPW) it is necessary to correctly specify the model. In AIPWs case, there is at least the chance to still be unbiased if one of the two models (outcome or balancing) is incorrect. Here, if the outcome model is incorrect, the balancing model will likely be incorrect too since they are fit jointly and rely on each other.
12) The authors should add the AIPW estimator to their comparison models since it is 1) well-known in the literature, 2) has some theoretical guarantees that most of the other comparison models don't have, 3) probably will do pretty well and is MUCH simpler than fitting an over-parametrized MLP model (after all, there are only 3-4 covariates in one of the sim studies).
13) The authors' explanation of the balancing loss is confusing. The interpretation of the g-weight terms isn't immediately obvious. One other way to phrase this might be as "we're imposing a constraint such that the learned representation achieves balance. In practice this is achieved by minimizing the squared deviation between a reweighed treated cohort and a reweighed untreated cohort. We chose these weights because ..."
14) Comparison with Dragonnet: the authors note that dragonnet has some consistency results. This method does not have such results, correct? Also, the authors should argue why the BCE loss does not sufficiently impose balance despite essentially fitting a propensity score.
15) Physical exercise data set: why do the authors switch to A corresponding to treatment?
16) What's the distribution of the outcome in the physical exercise data set? Only the mean is given.
17) "In our simulation, we also consider a fourth observation variable highly depending on the decision of treatment, the improvement in physical function X4, generated as independent normal variable with mean gamma*A and sd 2." <-- the authors claim that a real world study would mistakenly include this as a covariate and thus it helps demonstrate that their method achieves balance. That doesn't make sense to me. X4 is clearly a post treatment (mediator) variable. A practitioner with causal expertise would _know_ not to condition on a post-treatment variable. Owing to that observation, the experiments that rely on this variable would seem not to demonstrate the behavior the authors think they are.
18) Why us MAE rather than a squared error like PEHE? A squared residual forms the basis of your loss function so it makes sense to use it for evaluating performance.
19) It's not clear why the authors report a different train and test performance. What are train and test here? Generally in effect estimation contexts the goal is to simply estimate the effect on the data at hand, which means using ALL of the data since that is the most statistically efficient thing to do. If any data needs to be held out (e.g. for tuning hyperparameters), it is key that sample splitting (cross-val or methods like those described by Chernozukhov and Robins) be employed. It should be sufficient to simply fit the model, evaluate the effect and compare to the ground truth that is available due to the nature of the considered data sets.
To be clear: the goal of causal effect estimation is generally not out of sample prediction. It is a parameter estimation problem as in classical statistics.
20) Why are OLS/Logistic Regression only used in the Jobs data? Are the authors simply copying these results from another paper? It shouldn't be too hard to re-run those methods on the other data sets. Also, here is where AIPW should be included. In light of comment #19, it's not immediately clear that the proposed method is still "state of the art".
21) Where are the Table 1-style results for the exercise/depression data set? Based on the described data generating process in section 4.1, I'd expect linear regression and AIPW to do better than the proposed NN method since the outcome is (apparently?) Gaussian and AIPW with logistic regression for the propensity score and linear regression (correctly specified here) should converge faster (i.e. attain variance = fisher info matrix) than the data-hungry NN with many thousands of parameters.
22) Section 5.1 analysis: what was the observed Wasserstein distance between the treated and control groups (i.e. before applying the representation function g)? What is the distance when the "representation" is a simple re-weighing by propensity scores (observed or fit via logistic regression)?
23) Section 5.2: See the above comment about X4 being post-treatment. It doesn't seem appropriate to claim that the analysis here is measuring/addressing the difference between treatment and control _covariate_ distributions since X4 is only a "covariate" under sketchy terms (i.e. ignoring the fact that it is post-treatment which one wouldn't usually do in a properly run analysis).
24) Conclusion: the authors claim that they show their method's outperformance increases when there is a larger distance between the treatment and control groups. This is certainly not shown in the first set of experiments (i.e. Table 1), as distance between cohorts isn't considered. The second experiment talks about distances but doesn't actually measure performance of effect estimation. It is also flawed, as discussed above. Based on these points, it seems the authors can't claim this increasing or "widening" outperformance as a function of cohort distance.
22)
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

content.title: Response to Reviewer uhL3 (2/2)
content.comment:
14. The authors did not claim that Dragonnet has _consistency results_. Regarding why our objective achieves high similarity between learned treated and untreated distributions and why BCE is less effective, in appendix there are the sections A3 (“THE EFFECT OF BACK-PROPAGATING THE GRADIENT WITH RESPECT TO THE AUTO-BALANCING OBJECTIVE”) and A4 (“COMPARISON WITH THE BINARY CROSS-ENTROPY OBJECTIVE”), showing why if we adopt the former instead of the latter we have a lower upper bound of the expected error in learning ITE (Theorem 5) in case the treated and untreated covariate distributions are highly dissimilar, as unfortunately might happen for observational data. These are advanced topics and we had to put them in the appendix because of the constraint of max. 9 pages for the main part of the manuscript. 

15. The physical exercise synthetic dataset has been removed as per point #17

16. We reported the standard deviation of the outcome in the revised paper. 

17. We acknowledge that X4 is a post-treatment variable and, for this reason, we removed the physical exercise synthetic dataset, the related analysis and claims in the revised paper. 

18. For the Jobs dataset we cannot evaluate PEHE, since there is no ground truth for the ITE. In literature as evaluation metrics are used $\epsilon_{ATT}$ or $R_{POL}$. We selected  the former, as it is easier to understand and to communicate. For the IHDP dataset, there were both options, i.e. $\epsilon_{PEHE}$ and $\epsilon_{ATE}$. However, our comparator for this dataset is Dragonnet and in [2] the latter is adopted. In order to directly compare against previously developed models and to also demonstrate SOTA error rates for our model, we evaluated our model on the same metrics of our comparators. 

19. We understand that the goal of causal effect estimation is generally not out of sample prediction. However, our comparator on adopted datasets (IHDP and Jobs) reported train and test performance [2,5]. In order to directly compare against previously developed models and to also demonstrate SOTA error rates for our model, we maintained the same convention. 

20. Regarding _Why are OLS/Logistic Regression only used in the Jobs data? Are the authors simply copying these results from another paper?_ For each dataset, we replicated the performance of the SOTA and some other selected representation learning based models. As per point #12, AIPW has been included in the revised manuscript. 

21. The physical exercise synthetic dataset has been removed for the reasons of point #17. 

22. Prior Wasserstein distance has been included in the revised manuscript. Regarding the second question, the answer is in [4]. The point here is that re-weighting treated and untreated covariates by propensity score to compute ATE is not a representation learning approach, for which Theorem 5 is not applicable. 

23. The physical exercise synthetic dataset has been removed for the reasons of point #17. 

24. We removed such claim and we removed the physical exercise synthetic dataset as per point #17. 

Thanks again for your thoughtful review and helpful suggestions! We hope that our revised manuscript addresses your concerns and questions!

content.title: Response Following Rebuttal
content.comment:
I appreciate the authors making considerable efforts to address my concerns. Items 1-13 seem fine generally. With respect to AIPW, I think the authors could be more specific about what exactly they're doing (i.e., what nuisance models). The relative similarity in performance (especially "train" performance --- causal inference is a parameter estimation enterprise, not a prediction enterprise) adds to mine and the other reviewers' concerns about novelty. Essentially, what exactly is the delta? If the minimal added performance is coming at the cost of a complicated model that's generally harder to train and interpret I'm not sure the added performance is worth it. 

Still working through but I also wanted to comment on item 14 in case the author response period shuts down before I can properly respond. Forgive me for using the word consistency. I was inferring based on the authors' use of the words "optimal asymptotic properties" to describe Dragonnet". The authors also describe their method (section 3.3) as achieving "asymptotic robustness and efficiency" without proof. I'm not really sure why one would want an estimator that isn't consistent (i.e. it's asymptotically wrong) or what it would mean to be "robust and efficient" but not consistent. The authors should carefully consider this point and try to respond in the time allotted, if possible.

content.title: Continuing the above comments
content.comment:
Regarding comparisons (points 18 and 19): I realize it's valuable to compare apples-to-apples with the literature. If, however, the literature is choosing a poor convention, there's nothing that stops you from a) bucking that convention, and b) justifying to your readers that they should pay attention to the metric that is actually worth looking at from an estimation standpoint. Conventions can change! If your method looks worse when you're only looking at "training set" performance, it' ok to be transparent about it. We should also normalize presenting negative results.

20. If you're replicating (i.e., re-fitting the comparison models yourself), you should be able to also do that for the IHDP data. This isn't a rejection-worthy point but it doesn't really make sense to not include it. No need to do a new updated draft in the next day or so but it really does detract from the completeness of your results and should be les than an hour of work. If, on the other hand, you're copying the OLS results for the Jobs part of Table 1 from some other paper, you should cite that.

22. (edit: OpenReview keeps auto-changing the number to 21 for some reason. The following is in reference to point #22 from the above discussion) Got it, thank you. I think this could be highlighted a bit more clearly. I don't want to make the argument for you but I think this would be improved by explicitly pointing out "look, the distance is .1045 and then our balancing magic is working because the resulting distance is (something; it varies)". As above, I don't think it really make sense to look at Test. As in my original comment, I think it'd be useful to look at a naive balancing approach with vanilla propensity scores. It might do pretty well, in which case that's an argument against using a neural network. If it doesn't do well, that (along with the left-hand part of Table 3) should be ample argument to address the various concerns about novelty.

Cheers!

content.title: General Response to All Reviewers
content.comment:
We thank all the reviewers for their valuable comments and constructive feedback.  

We have revised the paper according to the suggestions and we summarize the highlights from the revision below and address each reviewer’s feedback separately as well:


* __Novelty and significance__: We acknowledge that our main contribution from this work has not been clearly articulated. Although our model improves upon the previously SOTA Dragonnet, our main finding is that what was previously considered a best practice when estimating propensity scores, which was the adoption of binary cross-entropy as objective, framing the problem as a supervised one, has been misunderstood to some extent and it is not supported by the early findings of Rosenbaum and Rubin (1983). In their seminal work, Rosenbaum and Rubin propose a framework for estimating treatment effects using propensity scores observed from the data while suggesting a model candidate (a logit model). Modeling the propensity scores in a supervised manner does not appear to be a main conclusion of their work. Their analysis aims at mimicking randomized control trials and a different optimization goal is more appropriate based on later work by [2], who discovered an upper bound on the expected error in learning ITEs for representation learning based models (Theorem 5). Our main contribution is reevaluating the original premise of propensity score modeling to closer mimicking randomized control trials and the use of representation learning techniques for achieving optimal results. Theorem 5 in our manuscript developed in [2], provided the theoretical justification for our analysis. In addition, 

    * in supplementary section A.2 (“THE EFFECT OF BACK-PROPAGATING THE GRADIENT WITH RESPECT TO THE AUTO-BALANCING OBJECTIVE”) is shown in detail how the back-propagation works with our self-supervised objective to achieve minimal dissimilarity between treated and untreated representations, 

    * while in supplementary section A.3 (“COMPARISON WITH THE BINARY CROSS-ENTROPY OBJECTIVE”) the comparison with binary cross-entropy is performed, showing why if we adopt the former instead of the latter we have a lower upper bound of the expected error in learning ITE (Theorem 5), in case the treated and untreated covariate distributions are highly dissimilar, as unfortunately might happen for observational data. 

    We have deeply revised our manuscript to better reflect our main contributions. We believe that representation learning is important when estimating heterogeneous treatment effects and that often changing the training objective can lead to significant changes in the learned representations. 

* __Ablation study and hyperparameter tuning__: We agree on the importance of hyperparameter tuning and, indeed, in the revised manuscript the section 5.1 (“Ablations”) is devoted to this purpose. In this section (Table 2) we evaluated different values of  

   * $\mathcal{\lambda}_{BAL}$   (relative importance of the self-supervised auto-balancing term), 

    * $\mathcal{\lambda}_{BCE}$    (relative importance of the binary cross-entropy term), 

    * $\mathcal{\lambda}_{TAR}$  (relative importance of the Dragonnet targeted regularization term) ,  

    * different activation functions (ReLU, ELU, Tanh)

    * different batch sizes and optimizers. 

    We proved empirically and highlighted that the best combination of hyperparameters are the ones reported in sect. 4.3. 

* __Hyperparameter tuning for Dragonnet__: To fairly compare different approaches, it is essential to tune the hyper-parameters of the baseline (Dragonnet in this case). Indeed, Table 2 includes also Dragonnet hyperparameter tuning, proving that its best results are worse in train/test accuracies compared to BCAUSS. However, the best hold-out result for Dragonnet in our analysis is significantly better than the one reported in the original paper [1]. 

* __AIPW__: besides the additional experiments for the ablation study (section 5.1 ), we added the AIPW estimator in the revised manuscript as a further comparator (Table 1).  

We hope our revised manuscript and additional experiments can provide further clarity. Please let us know if any improvement can be made!

Reference:

1. [Claudia Shi, David M. Blei, and Victor Veitch. Adapting neural networks for the estimation of treatment effects. In Hanna M. Wallach, Hugo Larochelle, Alina Beygelzimer, Florence d’Alche´ Buc, Emily B. Fox, and Roman Garnett (eds.), NeurIPS, pp. 2503–2513, 2019.](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2019/file/8fb5f8be2aa9d6c64a04e3ab9f63feee-Paper.pdf)

2. [Uri Shalit, Fredrik D. Johansson, and David Sontag. Estimating individual treatment effect: generalization bounds and algorithms. In Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Machine Learning, pp. 3076–3085, 2017](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v70/shalit17a/shalit17a.pdf)
